text: A model that aces its training data can still be a bad model. This lesson is about the two ways a model can fail, and they're opposites of each other.

This is straight from scikit-learn's own documentation: three polynomial models of increasing complexity, fit to the same noisy curve. Degree one is a straight line — too simple, it misses the curve and has the highest error. Degree four tracks the true curve closely. Degree fifteen bends itself into a wild, wiggly shape chasing every sample point, including the random noise in exactly where those points happened to land.

So there are three states a model can be in. Underfitting, too simple to capture the real pattern. A good fit, which captures the pattern without chasing noise. And overfitting, complex enough to memorize the training data's noise, not just its pattern.

You can't tell these apart from training performance alone — you need to compare it to performance on data the model never trained on. A big gap between train score and test score is the signature of overfitting. Both scores being mediocre, with no gap, is the signature of underfitting.

The fixes are opposites too. For underfitting: a more expressive model, better features, more training. For overfitting: a simpler model, more training data, or regularization — a technique that penalizes overly complex models, which we'll come back to.
Next, we'll look at the actual numbers behind "train score" and "test score" — the evaluation metrics you use to make that comparison in the first place.
